subject: A fast way to calculate the bivariate poisson in STAN

messages.author: 71c315ee557ff234
messages.subject: A fast way to calculate the bivariate poisson in STAN
parts:
For math details  and specification look in:

http://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/108705/deriving-the-bivariate-poisson-distribution

For speed reasons miny is used as a parameter: miny := min(r,s)
mu1, mu2, mu3 must be provided on log scale. 

The return value is the probability mass function of the bivariate poisson on the log scale. 

   real bipois2(int r,int s,real mu1,real mu2,real mu3,int miny);
 
   real bipois2(int r,int s,real mu1,real mu2,real mu3, int miny) {
     real ss;
     real log_s;
     real mus;

     ss <- poisson_log_log(r,mu1) + poisson_log_log(s,mu2) - exp(mu3);
     if(miny > 0) {
       mus <- -mu1-mu2+mu3;
       log_s <- ss;
       
       for(k in 1:miny) {
            log_s <- log_s + log(r - k + 1) + mus
                           + log(s - k + 1)
                           - log(k);
            ss <- log_sum_exp(ss, log_s);
       }
     }
     return(ss);
   }

Andre

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] A fast way to calculate the bivariate poisson in STAN
parts:
Cool. Thanks.

I'd recommend defining miny within the function call:

int miny;
...
miny <- min(r, s);

And presumably miny must be >= 0.

if (miny < 0)
reject("bipois arguments must be > 0, found r=", r, "; s=", s);

Then you don't have to worry about consistency of the inputs
and get the appropriate warning messages.

It's usually a bad idea to have an input that's a function of
other inputs unless absolutely necessary for speed; users will just
mess it up and curse you for having to write the min() themselves.
It's a very fast operation, here, so no worries about speed (you
could precompute miny otherwise).

If you could take an int[] argument for r and s, then you
could define it using our probability notation and use

rs ~ bipois(mu1, mu2, mu3);

Then you need to check rs size and there's some indexing overhead,
but it looks nice.

But given that mu is provided on the log scale, then our convention is
bipois_log, and we'd write log_mu for the params, so it'd look like:

rs ~ bipois_log(log_mu1, log_mu2, log_mu3);

- Bob

P.S. When Mitzi finishes the array expressions, we'll be able to write

{ a, b } ~ bipois_log(log_mu1, log_mu2, log_mu3);

P.P.S. We need some way to distribute useful user-defined functions
like this.
